title: Diwali (5 days — Dhanteras, Naraka Chaturdashi, Lakshmi puja, Govardhan, Bhai Dooj)
hook: a hill of food stacked before dawn: Lakshmi at the door, a mountain lifted, a sister's blessing
carry: Diwali (5 days — Dhanteras, Naraka Chaturdashi, Lakshmi puja, Govardhan, Bhai Dooj)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Diwali began: a clean house, something new on Dhanteras, a lamp for Yama, and Narakasura defeated before dawn. Did you clean one small corner? Day one hundred and forty.

The lamps from the big night are still smoking on the windowsills, and before dawn a temple kitchen is already roaring. Rice, lentils, vegetables, sweets, dish after dish, carried out in steel pans and stacked on the steps in front of the image, higher and higher, until the food is shaped like a small hill. Children wait for their share and hear the story while they wait: a boy who once lifted a real hill. And somewhere across town, a sister is already planning tomorrow's plate for her brother. The lamps were only the middle of Diwali. Today, the last three days.
screen: `BEFORE DAWN, A TEMPLE KITCHEN.` → `FOOD STACKED LIKE A HILL.` → `THE LAMPS WERE ONLY THE MIDDLE.`

segments.voice: Day three is Lakshmi puja, on the new moon itself, the night you met on day eighty-eight: the clean house, the open door, the little footprints walking in. Two things to add. Ganesha is honored beside Lakshmi, and first, as always: clear the road, then begin. And the same night is kept in other ways. In Bengal it belongs to Kali, the fierce mother. In Gujarat, the new year begins the next morning. Day four is Govardhan puja, the hill from this morning's kitchen. The story, from the Bhagavata Purana: young Krishna persuaded the cowherds of Vraj to honor their own hill, Govardhan, which fed their cows, instead of the storm god Indra. Indra, offended, sent rain for days. And Krishna lifted the whole hill with one hand, a single finger in many tellings, and held it up like an umbrella while everyone sheltered underneath. So temples build a mountain of food, called annakut, dish after dish, and share it. Day five is Bhai Dooj, for brothers and sisters. A sister marks her brother's forehead with a tilak, prays for his long life, and feeds him; he gives her a gift. The story behind it is that Yama, lord of death, visited his sister Yamuna on this day and was welcomed with a meal. Notice the bookends. Diwali opened with a lamp for Yama, asking death to pass by. It closes with Yama as a brother, sitting down to eat. Five days: a clean house, darkness beaten, fortune welcomed, shelter under a lifted mountain, and family at the table.
screen: `LAKSHMI PUJA: GANESHA FIRST.` · `GOVARDHAN: THE HILL HELD UP.` · `BHAI DOOJ: A SISTER'S BLESSING.` · `YAMA AT THE START AND AT THE END.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find the hill someone held up for you. Settle, and breathe. Think back to a stretch when things were pouring down on you, and someone held something up so you could get through: a parent who took the extra shift, a friend who covered for you, a teacher who stayed late. Picture them standing there, holding it. Breathe out slowly, under the shelter. Then let one more face come, someone who's like a brother or sister to you, and wish them a long life, the way a sister does on Bhai Dooj. The bell holds the time.
Diwali. Five days of light: something new, darkness defeated, Lakshmi welcomed on the darkest night, a mountain lifted, and siblings at the table. Today's word.

Your line: Diwali, five days: Dhanteras, Naraka Chaturdashi, Lakshmi puja, Govardhan, Bhai Dooj. Today, send one message to someone who's like a sibling to you, wishing them a long life. Day one hundred and forty.

howItsDone: On the new-moon night of Diwali many Hindu families perform Lakshmi puja with Ganesha, light lamps throughout the home and draw Lakshmi's footprints at the door; the next day temples offer annakut for Govardhan puja, and on Bhai Dooj sisters mark their brothers' foreheads with tilak and share a meal.

myth: Diwali's main night falls on the full moon

Ganesha is honored alongside Lakshmi on Diwali night
first, as always: clear the road, then begin.
Yama appears at both ends of Diwali
a lamp asks him to pass by on Dhanteras, and on Bhai Dooj he's a brother welcomed to a meal.

fork.setup: you're a cowherd in Vraj. the storm god is furious, and it's been pouring for days. the young Krishna says, come under here. what happens?
options: he leads everyone into a cave.
he lifts the whole hill to shelter them.
he asks Indra to stop the rain.
fork.reveal: he holds up Govardhan like an umbrella while everyone and their cows shelter underneath. temples remember it with annakut, a mountain of food.

original.note: Sanskrit lakṣmī: fortune, prosperity, well-being; the goddess welcomed on Diwali night.

trapdoor: what you thought: fireworks and sweets.
what it means: five days that move from a clean house to darkness defeated, fortune welcomed, shelter given and family fed.

what a scholar hears: Govardhan's lifting is told in Bhagavata Purana 10.24–25; the Yama–Yamuna story behind Bhai Dooj (Yama Dvitiya) is found in later Puranic and regional tradition; Bengal keeps Kali puja on the same new moon.

sources.ref: Lakshmi puja and Yama Dvitiya (Bhai Dooj), as kept in household and regional tradition

Editor review (2026-10-01): the hook opened 'Picture it from above' (a banned opener), called the new moon 'the brightest night of the year' (unsourced superlative), and repeated day 88's open-door-and-footprints scene almost line for line; the teach repeated day 88's footprints and account books. New hook opens on the annakut kitchen; the teach recalls day 88 in one line and adds Ganesha, Kali and the Gujarati new year. Govardhan: the Bhagavata (10.25) has Krishna hold the hill with one hand; 'a single finger' is now attributed to 'many tellings'. 'Hundreds of dishes' cut. The practice (a lamp at the door, as on days 81, 88 and 139) now uses the Govardhan shelter image and keeps the Bhai Dooj wish.
